papers.full_text: Angiopoietin-1/Tie2 Activation as a Therapeutic Hypothesis for 1 Hantavirus-Induced Vascular Permeability 2 Author: Atharv Dhore1 3 Affiliation: 1 Aldie, Virginia, USA 4 † Corresponding author: Atharv Dhore, anish.dhore@gmail.com 5 Abstract 6 Severe hantavirus infection produces extensive vascular leakage, driven by a combination of endothelial 7 dysfunction, dysregulated inflammation, VEGF-mediated hyperpermeability, angiopoietin imbalance, and 8 degradation of the endothelial glycocalyx. This narrative review draws on the peer-reviewed literature, with 9 particular attention to work published between 2016 and 2026, to examine how hantavirus-induced vascular 10 permeability arises in hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), 11 and how Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1)/Tie2 signaling and glycocalyx injury contribute to endothelial barrier failure. 12 Direct hantavirus evidence shows that Ang-1 inhibits hantavirus-directed endothelial permeability in vitro and that 13 angiopoietin dysregulation tracks with disease severity in patients; findings that Tie2 activation curbs vascular 14 leakage in sepsis and other non-hantavirus models are mechanistically suggestive but remain inferential rather than 15 hantavirus-specific. No hantavirus animal model or clinical trial has yet evaluated Ang-1/Tie2-directed therapy, so 16 this review treats the approach as a testable hypothesis rather than an established or recommended treatment; 17 confirming its therapeutic value will require dedicated hantavirus-specific animal and clinical studies. 18 Keywords: hantavirus, endothelial dysfunction, vascular permeability, angiopoietin; Tie2, therapeutic hypothesis 19 1. Introduction 20 Hantaviruses are negative-sense RNA viruses of the family Hantaviridae. They persist in chronically infected rodent 21 reservoirs (and, in a few species, shrews or moles) and reach humans mainly through inhalation of aerosolized 22 excreta. The Old World hantaviruses, among them Hantaan virus, Puumala virus, and Dobrava-Belgrade virus, 23 circulate across Europe and Asia and cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). The New World 24 hantaviruses, including Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus, circulate throughout the Americas and cause hantavirus 25 pulmonary syndrome (HPS); Andes virus is unusual among hantaviruses in that it can also spread person-to-person.1 26 Both syndromes share a core clinical picture, increased vascular permeability, thrombocytopenia, hypotension, and 27 multiorgan dysfunction, but differ in which organs bear the brunt of disease: HFRS chiefly affects the kidneys, while 28 HPS chiefly affects the lungs and heart, reflecting differences in which vascular beds each viral group preferentially 29 colonizes. Hantaviruses infect endothelial cells without lysing them outright; disease severity instead tracks with 30 disruption of endothelial barrier function.2 When that barrier fails badly enough, the result is pulmonary edema, 31 shock, renal failure, and death. 32 The two syndromes also differ sharply in how often they occur and how deadly they are. HFRS accounts for an 33 estimated 150,000-200,000 cases annually, most of them in Asia and Europe, with case fatality ranging from under 34 1% to roughly 15% depending on the causative virus.26 HPS is comparatively rare, with roughly 200 cases reported 35 each year across the Americas, but it carries a substantially higher case fatality rate of up to 50%. Neither syndrome 36 yet has an approved antiviral therapy or vaccine. This asymmetry (HFRS common but comparatively survivable, 37 HPS rare but often fatal) resurfaces throughout this review, since the direct clinical evidence bearing on the Ang- 38 1/Tie2 hypothesis is itself unevenly distributed between the two conditions. 39 The vascular leakage seen in hantavirus infection arises from an interplay of viral infection, inflammatory cytokines, 40 vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, angiopoietin dysregulation, and glycocalyx degradation.3 41 Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1) is an endothelial-stabilizing ligand that activates the Tie2 receptor tyrosine kinase, 42 promoting endothelial quiescence, reinforcing the barrier, and dampening inflammatory signaling.4 Angiopoietin-2 43 (Ang-2) works in the opposite direction, destabilizing the vessel wall. 44 This paper is a narrative literature review that builds toward a therapeutic hypothesis, not an original experimental or 45 clinical study. It traces the molecular mechanisms behind hantavirus-induced endothelial dysfunction, with emphasis 46 on VEGF signaling, Ang-1/Tie2 pathway activity, IL-6 trans-signaling, angiopoietin imbalance, and glycocalyx 47 degradation, while distinguishing evidence gathered directly from hantavirus systems from evidence inferred from 48 related conditions such as sepsis and dengue. Sections 3 through 6 work through each mechanistic pathway in turn; 49 Section 7 draws this evidence together into an explicit direct-versus-inferential summary (Table 1) and lays out 50 concrete next steps and candidate experimental systems; Sections 8 and 9 address the review's limitations and state 51 its overall hypothesis. The central question is whether endothelial stabilization through Ang-1/Tie2 signaling, 52 together with the related pathways discussed alongside it, is a biologically plausible direction for hantavirus 53 research, while keeping hantavirus-specific evidence clearly separated from evidence borrowed from other diseases. 54 2. Literature Review Methodology 55 This review relies on a narrative approach to develop a therapeutic hypothesis. It is not a systematic review or meta- 56 analysis; a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram was not used, since the aim was to synthesize mechanistic and clinical 57 evidence rather than to pool results exhaustively. No original experiments, patient data, animal studies, or clinical 58 trial data were generated for this manuscript. 59 Literature was identified through structured searches of three databases, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of 60 Science, conducted on July 23, 2026 and restricted to English-language, peer-reviewed sources. The following 61 title/abstract/keyword search strings were used, combined with Boolean AND/OR operators: 62 1. ("hantavirus" OR "orthohantavirus" OR "Puumala virus" OR "Hantaan virus" OR "Andes virus" OR "Sin 63 Nombre virus") AND ("vascular permeability" OR "endothelial dysfunction" OR "capillary leak") 64 2. ("hantavirus" OR "hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome" OR "HFRS" OR "hantavirus pulmonary syndrome" 65 OR "HPS") AND ("angiopoietin" OR "Tie2" OR "Ang-1" OR "Ang-2") 66 3. ("hantavirus") AND ("VEGF" OR "vascular endothelial growth factor" OR "VE-cadherin") 67 4. ("hantavirus" OR "HFRS" OR "HPS") AND ("glycocalyx" OR "syndecan" OR "heparan sulfate") 68 5. ("angiopoietin" OR "Tie2 agonist" OR "vasculotide") AND ("sepsis" OR "acute lung injury" OR "dengue") AND 69 ("vascular leak" OR "endothelial permeability") 70 Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance to hantavirus pathogenesis, endothelial or vascular biology, and 71 angiopoietin/Tie2/glycocalyx signaling; full texts of potentially relevant records were then examined. 72 Records were included if they were peer-reviewed original research or review articles addressing (a) hantavirus 73 clinical disease or pathogenesis, (b) endothelial barrier or vascular permeability mechanisms relevant to VEGF, 74 angiopoietin/Tie2, or glycocalyx biology, or (c) Tie2-agonist or endothelial-stabilizing interventions in any disease 75 model, the last of these retained specifically to support explicitly labeled inferential, non-hantavirus, mechanistic 76 claims. 77 Records were excluded if they were non-peer-reviewed (news articles, general websites, blog posts), conference 78 abstracts without an accompanying peer-reviewed publication, or of unclear or unverifiable peer-review status. 79 The initial exploratory search considered literature published between 1996 and 2026, but the reference base for this 80 manuscript emphasizes peer-reviewed sources from 2016 to 2026. A small number of earlier, foundational studies 81 are retained regardless, for example the 2008 in vitro demonstration that Ang-1 inhibits hantavirus-directed 82 endothelial permeability,6 the 2000 report that Ang-1 protects the adult vasculature against plasma leakage,11 and the 83 2013 identification of kallikrein-kinin system activation in hantavirus-infected endothelium,21 because they remain 84 the primary direct evidence for specific mechanistic claims and no more recent hantavirus-specific study has 85 superseded them. Each pre-2016 source retained on this basis is flagged as such at its first mention in the text. 86 The final evidence base comprises 26 references (see References). Throughout, this review distinguishes findings 87 obtained directly in hantavirus-infected cells, animals, or patients (direct evidence) from findings obtained in non- 88 hantavirus systems such as sepsis or dengue that are mechanistically relevant but untested in hantavirus infection 89 (inferential evidence); this distinction is flagged at each relevant claim in Sections 3-7 and summarized in Table 1. 90 3. Hantavirus Pathogenesis and Endothelial Dysfunction 91 Hantaviruses target the vascular endothelial cells lining capillaries and small blood vessels by binding beta-3 92 integrins, an interaction that facilitates viral entry and reshapes intracellular signaling.5 Beta-3 integrins normally 93 restrain VEGFR2 signaling and so act as negative regulators of VEGF-driven permeability; pathogenic hantaviruses 94 disable this restraint, and the resulting loss of integrin-mediated control is the proposed link between hantavirus 95 infection and the VEGF hyperresponsiveness discussed in Section 4. Even as the virus replicates successfully inside 96 endothelial cells, those cells remain structurally intact, so the vascular leakage that follows reflects altered 97 endothelial function rather than direct viral cytotoxicity. This distinguishes hantavirus-induced vascular leak from 98 the cytolytic viral hemorrhagic fevers and supports pursuing host-response-directed therapy alongside antiviral 99 approaches. 100 Capillary leakage and endothelial dysfunction underlie the clinical picture in both HFRS and HPS. As vascular 101 permeability rises, plasma and cells escape into surrounding tissue, producing pulmonary edema, hypovolemia, 102 hypotension, and organ dysfunction.3 Immune activation contributes substantially to disease severity, particularly 103 through cytokine-driven endothelial activation, discussed in detail in Section 3.1. The kallikrein-kinin system also 104 contributes directly to hantavirus-induced permeability: infected endothelial cells show increased factor XII and 105 kallikrein activity along with bradykinin release, and bradykinin in turn promotes vasodilation and vascular 106 permeability in this setting.21 107 3.1 Cytokine-Driven Endothelial Activation: IL-6 Trans-Signaling 108 Direct hantavirus evidence ties elevated cytokines to endothelial dysfunction and disease severity. In a cohort of 64 109 patients hospitalized with acute Puumala virus infection, serum IL-2, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, and TGF-β1 were 110 significantly elevated relative to healthy controls, both early and late in the course of acute disease.23 IL-6 has since 111 emerged as a biomarker of HFRS and HPS severity, though until recently the mechanism linking it to endothelial 112 barrier failure was unclear. 113 A 2025 study closed that gap. IL-6 signals through two distinct routes: classical signaling, generally protective and 114 dependent on a membrane-bound IL-6 receptor that endothelial cells largely lack, and trans-signaling, mediated by a 115 soluble IL-6 receptor (sIL-6R) paired with the ubiquitous gp130 co-receptor, which can drive pathogenic responses 116 even in receptor-poor cell types such as endothelium. Using primary human endothelial cells infected with Puumala 117 virus and treated with recombinant sIL-6R, the study found that infection stimulates IL-6 secretion and that IL-6 118 trans-signaling, not classical signaling, drives endothelial barrier dysfunction in vitro. In plasma from 28 patients 119 with acute PUUV-associated HFRS, IL-6 trans-signaling potential correlated with markers of clinical severity, 120 including serum creatinine and thrombocytopenia.22 This is, to date, the most direct mechanistic link between a 121 hantavirus-elevated cytokine and endothelial barrier failure demonstrated in both an infected-cell system and 122 hantavirus patients, and it identifies IL-6 trans-signaling as a fourth hantavirus-validated pathway relevant to 123 endothelial-stabilizing therapy, alongside VEGF, Ang-1/Tie2, and glycocalyx degradation. As with the angiopoietin 124 data discussed in Section 5, however, this direct clinical evidence comes specifically from PUUV-associated HFRS 125 and has not yet been established for HPS. 126 4. VEGF-Mediated Endothelial Hyperpermeability 127 Vascular endothelial growth factor is a potent regulator of endothelial permeability.7 VEGF binds VEGFR2 on 128 endothelial cells and activates Src-family kinases that disrupt adherens junction proteins, including vascular 129 endothelial (VE)-cadherin.8 Loss of VE-cadherin weakens endothelial junctions and raises paracellular permeability. 130 Pathogenic hantaviruses sensitize endothelial cells to VEGF-induced permeability, so that infected cells respond far 131 more strongly to VEGF stimulation than uninfected ones.9 VEGF-driven phosphorylation of VE-cadherin widens 132 endothelial gaps and increases plasma leakage, and infected endothelial cells progressively downregulate VE- 133 cadherin in response.10 134 Unlike the angiopoietin and IL-6 trans-signaling evidence discussed in Sections 5 and 3.1, direct clinical evidence 135 for VEGF-driven permeability spans both hantavirus syndromes rather than just one. In HFRS, serum VEGF is 136 elevated and correlates with reduced soluble VEGFR2 during the acute phase of Hantaan virus infection.9 In HPS, 137 VEGF is similarly elevated in pulmonary edema fluid and peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients with 138 acute Andes-virus-associated disease.24 Of the four mechanisms reviewed here (VEGF, Ang-1/Tie2, glycocalyx, IL- 139 6), VEGF is therefore the only one with direct human evidence in both HFRS and HPS, giving it broader direct 140 support than the other pathways discussed (Table 1). 141 5. Angiopoietin-1/Tie2 Signaling Pathway 142 The angiopoietin-Tie2 pathway governs endothelial stability and vascular integrity. Ang-1 binds and activates the 143 Tie2 receptor tyrosine kinase on endothelial cells, clustering Tie2 at cell-cell junctions and triggering downstream 144 PI3K/Akt signaling; this cascade phosphorylates and inactivates the forkhead transcription factor FOXO1, stabilizes 145 junctional complexes, supports endothelial survival and tight junction maintenance, sets anti-inflammatory signaling 146 in motion, and suppresses vascular leakage.4 Consistent with this broader vascular-protective role, Ang-1 has been 147 shown to protect the adult vasculature against plasma leakage,11 and, in direct hantavirus evidence from an in vitro 148 permeability assay, Ang-1 significantly inhibits hantavirus-directed endothelial permeability at physiologic 149 concentrations.6 150 Ang-2 works against this system, destabilizing blood vessels and antagonizing Tie2 signaling. Endothelial cells 151 release Ang-2 rapidly from Weibel-Palade bodies during inflammation and infection,13 and elevated Ang-2 152 promotes endothelial activation and greater vascular leak. In direct clinical hantavirus evidence, a cohort of 31 153 patients with acute Puumala virus infection and one patient with Dobrava-Belgrade (Sochi) virus infection showed 154 an elevated Ang-2/Ang-1 ratio relative to controls, and this imbalance correlated with markers of disease severity, 155 including serum creatinine and thrombocyte levels.12 An important caveat applies here: both patient groups 156 contributing this direct clinical evidence had HFRS rather than HPS, and no comparable human angiopoietin dataset 157 yet exists for HPS. Angiopoietin imbalance is not unique to hantavirus infection; similar Ang-2-driven vascular 158 instability has been described across other host-response-mediated inflammatory syndromes, which lends inferential 159 support to host-directed endothelial stabilization across inflammatory vascular leak syndromes generally, though it 160 remains inferential rather than direct hantavirus evidence.20 161 Tie2-targeting therapeutics have shown efficacy in non-hantavirus experimental models of vascular leak. In murine 162 sepsis, Tie2 activation reduces cytokine elevation, glycocalyx degradation, vascular leakage, and organ damage, a 163 finding from a sepsis model, not a hantavirus one.14 Vasculotide, a synthetic Tie2 agonist peptide, similarly reduces 164 mortality and vascular permeability in murine sepsis models, again in a non-hantavirus system.15 These studies make 165 Tie2 activation a biologically plausible endothelial-stabilizing strategy, but neither vasculotide nor any other Tie2 166 agonist has yet been tested in a hantavirus model. 167 6. Glycocalyx Degradation and Endothelial Barrier Failure 168 The endothelial glycocalyx is a carbohydrate-rich layer coating endothelial cells, built from glycoproteins, 169 proteoglycans, syndecans, and glycosaminoglycans such as heparan sulfate and hyaluronan.16 It regulates vascular 170 permeability, mechanotransduction, leukocyte adhesion, and plasma protein retention; when it is damaged, 171 endothelial permeability rises and vascular leak syndromes worsen. 172 Inflammation, oxidative stress, cytokines, and angiopoietin dysregulation all induce glycocalyx shedding, largely by 173 activating matrix metalloproteinases and heparanase, which cleave membrane-bound proteoglyc…

full_text_sections.full_text: Angiopoietin-1/Tie2 Activation as a Therapeutic Hypothesis for 1 Hantavirus-Induced Vascular Permeability 2 Author: Atharv Dhore1 3 Affiliation: 1 Aldie, Virginia, USA 4 † Corresponding author: Atharv Dhore, anish.dhore@gmail.com 5 Abstract 6 Severe hantavirus infection produces extensive vascular leakage, driven by a combination of endothelial 7 dysfunction, dysregulated inflammation, VEGF-mediated hyperpermeability, angiopoietin imbalance, and 8 degradation of the endothelial glycocalyx. This narrative review draws on the peer-reviewed literature, with 9 particular attention to work published between 2016 and 2026, to examine how hantavirus-induced vascular 10 permeability arises in hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), 11 and how Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1)/Tie2 signaling and glycocalyx injury contribute to endothelial barrier failure. 12 Direct hantavirus evidence shows that Ang-1 inhibits hantavirus-directed endothelial permeability in vitro and that 13 angiopoietin dysregulation tracks with disease severity in patients; findings that Tie2 activation curbs vascular 14 leakage in sepsis and other non-hantavirus models are mechanistically suggestive but remain inferential rather than 15 hantavirus-specific. No hantavirus animal model or clinical trial has yet evaluated Ang-1/Tie2-directed therapy, so 16 this review treats the approach as a testable hypothesis rather than an established or recommended treatment; 17 confirming its therapeutic value will require dedicated hantavirus-specific animal and clinical studies. 18 Keywords: hantavirus, endothelial dysfunction, vascular permeability, angiopoietin; Tie2, therapeutic hypothesis 19 1. Introduction 20 Hantaviruses are negative-sense RNA viruses of the family Hantaviridae. They persist in chronically infected rodent 21 reservoirs (and, in a few species, shrews or moles) and reach humans mainly through inhalation of aerosolized 22 excreta. The Old World hantaviruses, among them Hantaan virus, Puumala virus, and Dobrava-Belgrade virus, 23 circulate across Europe and Asia and cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). The New World 24 hantaviruses, including Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus, circulate throughout the Americas and cause hantavirus 25 pulmonary syndrome (HPS); Andes virus is unusual among hantaviruses in that it can also spread person-to-person.1 26 Both syndromes share a core clinical picture, increased vascular permeability, thrombocytopenia, hypotension, and 27 multiorgan dysfunction, but differ in which organs bear the brunt of disease: HFRS chiefly affects the kidneys, while 28 HPS chiefly affects the lungs and heart, reflecting differences in which vascular beds each viral group preferentially 29 colonizes. Hantaviruses infect endothelial cells without lysing them outright; disease severity instead tracks with 30 disruption of endothelial barrier function.2 When that barrier fails badly enough, the result is pulmonary edema, 31 shock, renal failure, and death. 32 The two syndromes also differ sharply in how often they occur and how deadly they are. HFRS accounts for an 33 estimated 150,000-200,000 cases annually, most of them in Asia and Europe, with case fatality ranging from under 34 1% to roughly 15% depending on the causative virus.26 HPS is comparatively rare, with roughly 200 cases reported 35 each year across the Americas, but it carries a substantially higher case fatality rate of up to 50%. Neither syndrome 36 yet has an approved antiviral therapy or vaccine. This asymmetry (HFRS common but comparatively survivable, 37 HPS rare but often fatal) resurfaces throughout this review, since the direct clinical evidence bearing on the Ang- 38 1/Tie2 hypothesis is itself unevenly distributed between the two conditions. 39 The vascular leakage seen in hantavirus infection arises from an interplay of viral infection, inflammatory cytokines, 40 vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, angiopoietin dysregulation, and glycocalyx degradation.3 41 Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1) is an endothelial-stabilizing ligand that activates the Tie2 receptor tyrosine kinase, 42 promoting endothelial quiescence, reinforcing the barrier, and dampening inflammatory signaling.4 Angiopoietin-2 43 (Ang-2) works in the opposite direction, destabilizing the vessel wall. 44 This paper is a narrative literature review that builds toward a therapeutic hypothesis, not an original experimental or 45 clinical study. It traces the molecular mechanisms behind hantavirus-induced endothelial dysfunction, with emphasis 46 on VEGF signaling, Ang-1/Tie2 pathway activity, IL-6 trans-signaling, angiopoietin imbalance, and glycocalyx 47 degradation, while distinguishing evidence gathered directly from hantavirus systems from evidence inferred from 48 related conditions such as sepsis and dengue. Sections 3 through 6 work through each mechanistic pathway in turn; 49 Section 7 draws this evidence together into an explicit direct-versus-inferential summary (Table 1) and lays out 50 concrete next steps and candidate experimental systems; Sections 8 and 9 address the review's limitations and state 51 its overall hypothesis. The central question is whether endothelial stabilization through Ang-1/Tie2 signaling, 52 together with the related pathways discussed alongside it, is a biologically plausible direction for hantavirus 53 research, while keeping hantavirus-specific evidence clearly separated from evidence borrowed from other diseases. 54 2. Literature Review Methodology 55 This review relies on a narrative approach to develop a therapeutic hypothesis. It is not a systematic review or meta- 56 analysis; a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram was not used, since the aim was to synthesize mechanistic and clinical 57 evidence rather than to pool results exhaustively. No original experiments, patient data, animal studies, or clinical 58 trial data were generated for this manuscript. 59 Literature was identified through structured searches of three databases, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of 60 Science, conducted on July 23, 2026 and restricted to English-language, peer-reviewed sources. The following 61 title/abstract/keyword search strings were used, combined with Boolean AND/OR operators: 62 1. ("hantavirus" OR "orthohantavirus" OR "Puumala virus" OR "Hantaan virus" OR "Andes virus" OR "Sin 63 Nombre virus") AND ("vascular permeability" OR "endothelial dysfunction" OR "capillary leak") 64 2. ("hantavirus" OR "hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome" OR "HFRS" OR "hantavirus pulmonary syndrome" 65 OR "HPS") AND ("angiopoietin" OR "Tie2" OR "Ang-1" OR "Ang-2") 66 3. ("hantavirus") AND ("VEGF" OR "vascular endothelial growth factor" OR "VE-cadherin") 67 4. ("hantavirus" OR "HFRS" OR "HPS") AND ("glycocalyx" OR "syndecan" OR "heparan sulfate") 68 5. ("angiopoietin" OR "Tie2 agonist" OR "vasculotide") AND ("sepsis" OR "acute lung injury" OR "dengue") AND 69 ("vascular leak" OR "endothelial permeability") 70 Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance to hantavirus pathogenesis, endothelial or vascular biology, and 71 angiopoietin/Tie2/glycocalyx signaling; full texts of potentially relevant records were then examined. 72 Records were included if they were peer-reviewed original research or review articles addressing (a) hantavirus 73 clinical disease or pathogenesis, (b) endothelial barrier or vascular permeability mechanisms relevant to VEGF, 74 angiopoietin/Tie2, or glycocalyx biology, or (c) Tie2-agonist or endothelial-stabilizing interventions in any disease 75 model, the last of these retained specifically to support explicitly labeled inferential, non-hantavirus, mechanistic 76 claims. 77 Records were excluded if they were non-peer-reviewed (news articles, general websites, blog posts), conference 78 abstracts without an accompanying peer-reviewed publication, or of unclear or unverifiable peer-review status. 79 The initial exploratory search considered literature published…

analysis.background: Severe hantavirus infection produces extensive vascular leakage driven by endothelial dysfunction, dysregulated inflammation, VEGF‑mediated hyperpermeability, angiopoietin imbalance, and glycocalyx degradation. (A1)
analysis.main_directions: The narrative review (2016‑2026) examines how vascular permeability arises in HFRS and HPS and evaluates Ang‑1/Tie2 signaling and glycocalyx injury as mechanistic targets. (A2)
analysis.current_state: Direct hantavirus evidence shows Ang‑1 inhibits endothelial permeability in vitro and angiopoietin dysregulation correlates with disease severity in patients. (A3)
analysis.gaps: Tie2 activation reduces leakage in sepsis and other non‑hantavirus models, but this remains inferential for hantavirus, and no hantavirus‑specific animal or clinical studies have tested the approach. (A4)
analysis.future_research: Dedicated hantavirus animal models and clinical trials assessing Ang‑1/Tie2‑directed therapy are needed to validate its therapeutic potential. (A5)

analysis.summary_en: Background: Severe hantavirus infection causes extensive vascular leakage via endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, VEGF, angiopoietin imbalance, and glycocalyx loss. Main directions: The review synthesizes 2016‑2026 literature on permeability mechanisms in HFRS/HPS and the role of Ang‑1/Tie2 and glycocalyx injury. Current state: In vitro data show Ang‑1 reduces hantavirus‑induced permeability and patient studies link angiopoietin dysregulation to severity. Gaps: Tie2 activation benefits are inferred from sepsis models and no hantavirus‑specific animal or clinical trials exist. Future research: Conduct hantavirus‑specific animal experiments and clinical trials to test Ang‑1/Tie2 activation as a therapy.

papers.full_text: L’infection à hantavirus est une maladie à déclaration obligatoire au CanadaEn moyenne, 4 ou 5 cas d’infection à hantavirus sont confirmés chaque année au Canada. Dans presque tous les cas, la maladie est contractée en milieu agricole au Manitoba, en Saskatchewan, en Alberta et en Colombie-Britannique1. La transmission s’effectue généralement par contact avec des rongeurs infectés ou leurs excréments. Toutefois, l’espèce des Andes se distingue par sa capacité à être transmise entre personnes, généralement à la suite de contacts étroits et prolongés2. Les hantavirus causent 2 syndromes cliniquesLes espèces endémiques aux Amériques, y compris le virus des Andes, causent le syndrome cardiopulmonaire à hantavirus (SCPH), alors que les espèces européennes et asiatiques entraînent une fièvre hémorragique avec syndrome rénal (FHSR). Dans les 2 cas, la maladie se manifeste généralement après une incubation de 2 à 4 semaines, la médiane étant de 18 jours pour l’espèce des Andes. Le SCPH et la FHSR se manifestent d’abord par de la fièvre, des céphalées, une myalgie et des douleurs abdominales. Par la suite, le SCPH évolue vers un œdème pulmonaire, une insuffisance respiratoire, puis un choc cardiogénique, avec un taux de létalité de 12 % à 45 %. En revanche, la FHSR se caractérise par une insuffisance rénale aiguë et des manifestations hémorragiques (p. ex., épistaxis, hématurie, saignements gastro-intestinaux), avec un taux de létalité de 1 % à 12 %2,3. La sérologie et le test par amplification en chaîne par polymérase (ACP) s’effectuent au Laboratoire national de microbiologieLa présence d’anticorps de type immunoglobuline (Ig) M, une multiplication par au moins 4 du titre d’IgG ou la détection d’un hantavirus dans des échantillons sanguins analysés par ACP confirme l’infection à hantavirus. Le dépistage sérologique demeure la méthode diagnostique de préférence, alors que l’ACP est généralement utile dans la phase aiguë de l’infection1. On doit procéder à ces méthodes de dépistage sous la gouverne d’un ou d’une microbiologiste. Le traitement repose sur des mesures de soutienIl n’existe aucun vaccin ou traitement antiviral contre l’infection à hantavirus. Des études menées sur des animaux permettent de croire qu’on pourrait utiliser la ribavirine et le favipiravir tant pour le traitement que pour la prophylaxie postexposition4,5. On doit transférer les personnes chez qui on soupçonne un SCPH dans un établissement hospitalier doté de dispositifs d’oxygénation par membrane extracorporelle. Il est essentiel d’adopter des mesures préventives et de lutte contre les infections en cas de soupçon d’infection par le virus des AndesOn doit isoler toutes les personnes chez qui une infection par le virus des Andes est soupçonnée ou confirmée et prendre toutes les précautions contre la transmission par voie aérienne, par gouttelettes et par contact. Il faut également obtenir une consultation en infectiologie et aviser les autorités de santé publique locales6.Le JAMC vous invite à soumettre vos textes pour la rubrique « Cinq choses à savoir... » en ligne à https://mc.manuscriptcentral.com/cmaj. full_text_sections.other: L’infection à hantavirus est une maladie à déclaration obligatoire au CanadaEn moyenne, 4 ou 5 cas d’infection à hantavirus sont confirmés chaque année au Canada. Dans presque tous les cas, la maladie est contractée en milieu agricole au Manitoba, en Saskatchewan, en Alberta et en Colombie-Britannique1. La transmission s’effectue généralement par contact avec des rongeurs infectés ou leurs excréments. Toutefois, l’espèce des Andes se distingue par sa capacité à être transmise entre personnes, généralement à la suite de contacts étroits et prolongés2. Les hantavirus causent 2 syndromes cliniquesLes espèces endémiques aux Amériques, y compris le virus des Andes, causent le syndrome cardiopulmonaire à hantavirus (SCPH), alors que les espèces européennes et asiatiques entraînent une fièvre hémorragique avec syndrome rénal (FHSR). Dans les 2 cas, la maladie se manifeste généralement après une incubation de 2 à 4 semaines, la médiane étant de 18 jours pour l’espèce des Andes. Le SCPH et la FHSR se manifestent d’abord par de la fièvre, des céphalées, une myalgie et des douleurs abdominales. Par la suite, le SCPH évolue vers un œdème pulmonaire, une insuffisance respiratoire, puis un choc cardiogénique, avec un taux de létalité de 12 % à 45 %. En revanche, la FHSR se caractérise par une insuffisance rénale aiguë et des manifestations hémorragiques (p. ex., épistaxis, hématurie, saignements gastro-intestinaux), avec un taux de létalité de 1 % à 12 %2,3. La sérologie et le test par amplification en chaîne par polymérase (ACP) s’effectuent au Laboratoire national de microbiologieLa présence d’anticorps de type immunoglobuline (Ig) M, une multiplication par au moins 4 du titre d’IgG ou la détection d’un hantavirus dans des échantillons sanguins analysés par ACP confirme l’infection à hantavirus. Le dépistage sérologique demeure la méthode diagnostique de préférence, alors que l’ACP est généralement utile dans la phase aiguë de l’infection1. On doit procéder à ces méthodes de dépistage sous la gouverne d’un ou d’une microbiologiste. Le traitement repose sur des mesures de soutienIl n’existe aucun vaccin ou traitement antiviral contre l’infection à hantavirus. Des études menées sur des animaux permettent de croire qu’on pourrait utiliser la ribavirine et le favipiravir tant pour le traitement que pour la prophylaxie postexposition4,5. On doit transférer les personnes chez qui on soupçonne un SCPH dans un établissement hospitalier doté de dispositifs d’oxygénation par membrane extracorporelle. Il est essentiel d’adopter des mesures préventives et de lutte contre les infections en cas de soupçon d’infection par le virus des AndesOn doit isoler toutes les personnes chez qui une infection par le virus des Andes est soupçonnée ou confirmée et prendre toutes les précautions contre la transmission par voie aérienne, par gouttelettes et par contact. Il faut également obtenir une consultation en infectiologie et aviser les autorités de santé publique locales6.Le JAMC vous invite à soumettre vos textes pour la rubrique « Cinq choses à savoir... » en ligne à https://mc.manuscriptcentral.com/cmaj. analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is a notifiable disease in Canada, with an average of 4–5 confirmed cases per year, most acquired in agricultural settings in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, transmitted mainly via contact with infected rodents or their excreta, while Andes virus can spread between people after close, prolonged contact.
analysis.methods: not reported in the supplied evidence

analysis.contribution: Provides a concise clinical and public‑health overview of hantavirus in Canada, outlining presentation, diagnostic algorithms, supportive‑care recommendations, and infection‑control precautions for Andes virus, thereby guiding clinicians and health authorities.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is a notifiable disease in Canada with 4–5 annual cases, mainly acquired in agricultural areas and transmitted via rodents, though Andes virus can spread person‑to‑person. Methods: not reported in the supplied evidence. Results: Incubation 2–4 weeks (median 18 days for Andes); cardiopulmonary syndrome mortality 12–45 %, hemorrhagic‑renal syndrome 1–12 %; diagnosis by IgM, ≥4‑fold IgG rise or PCR; no approved vaccine or antiviral, but ribavirin and favipiravir are promising in animals. Contribution: Summarizes clinical features, diagnostics, supportive care, and infection‑control measures for Canadian clinicians and public‑health officials. Limitations: Narrative overview without original data; only abstract/partial text available, limiting detail and broader applicability.

papers.title: Hantavirus mutagenesis is impacted by mutagens and host antiviral proteins
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic viruses that infect humans with high fatality rates. We currently have a poor understanding of the processes that contribute to hantavirus mutagenesis and therefore the potential for viral adaptation. To understand the drivers of mutations in hantaviruses, we calculated and compared mutational spectra across 14 divergent hantavirus species. We found that mutagens that are conserved across host species have a major impact on hantaviruses mutagenesis, contributing to at least six of the 12 possible mutation types. We found differences in mutational signatures across hantaviruses, some of which may be due to variation in host mutagen levels that are known to influence somatic mutations. However, we could find no evidence for differential mutational signatures between viruses associated with distinct diseases in humans and no evidence of tissue tropism differences between reservoir hosts. Using a novel method to quantify the impact of ZAP-mediated selection, we found that ZAP greatly influences mutational patterns in transition mutation types across hantaviruses. We also find evidence that APOBEC family proteins drive mutagenesis in all hantaviruses, with the likely exception of Nova virus. Our results therefore provide strong support that mutagens and host antiviral proteins are major contributors to hantavirus mutagenesis, thereby generating the genetic diversity necessary for viral adaptation.

full_text_sections.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic viruses that infect humans with high fatality rates. We currently have a poor understanding of the processes that contribute to hantavirus mutagenesis and therefore the potential for viral adaptation. To understand the drivers of mutations in hantaviruses, we calculated and compared mutational spectra across 14 divergent hantavirus species. We found that mutagens that are conserved across host species have a major impact on hantaviruses mutagenesis, contributing to at least six of the 12 possible mutation types. We found differences in mutational signatures across hantaviruses, some of which may be due to variation in host mutagen levels that are known to influence somatic mutations. However, we could find no evidence for differential mutational signatures between viruses associated with distinct diseases in humans and no evidence of tissue tropism differences between reservoir hosts. Using a novel method to quantify the impact of ZAP-mediated selection, we found that ZAP greatly influences mutational patterns in transition mutation types across hantaviruses. We also find evidence that APOBEC family proteins drive mutagenesis in all hantaviruses, with the likely exception of Nova virus. Our results therefore provide strong support that mutagens and host antiviral proteins are major contributors to hantavirus mutagenesis, thereby generating the genetic diversity necessary for viral adaptation.

papers.title: Characteristics and Superspreading Potential of Andes Virus Person-to-Person Transmission.
papers.abstract: By using historical contact tracing data, we estimated that 23.4% of case-patients caused 80% of Andes virus (ANDV) person-to-person transmission. We demonstrated a low but nonnegligible probability of observing a large-scale ANDV infection outbreak in a rodent-free setting consisting of close contacts, despite the historically self-limited person-to-person transmission of ANDV.

papers.title: Spatial-temporal distribution characteristics of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in 31 provinces and municipalities of P.R. China and multi-factorial prediction of incidence.
papers.abstract: Objective To integrate multi-source spatiotemporal data and construct an HFRS incidence prediction model using XGBoost with SHAP, exploring factors associated with HFRS incidence in China. Methods Collected HFRS case data from 31 provinces in China (2005-2020) and multi-source data on climate, land use, and population. Used MaxEnt to analyze rodent distribution and key environmental variables. Constructed an XGBoost model integrating climate, land use, host, and socio-economic features, with SHAP values assessing feature contributions. Dataset divided into training (70%), validation (15%), and test (15%) sets, with higher weights for high-incidence provinces. Results The reported HFRS cases in mainland China decreased from 2005 to 2020 but showed seasonal peaks. Cases were mainly among adults aged 20-60 years. The distribution of virus-carrying rodents was mainly affected by minimum temperature of the coldest month and elevation. After removing temporal features, land-use types (forest, cropland, shrub) showed greater relative importance than climate variables. Conclusion Forest, shrub, and cropland may affect disease transmission via host distribution and food availability. Climate factors act indirectly on HFRS risk. Temporal features remain critical for incidence prediction, while land use and rodent habitats are key exogenous drivers. These findings support targeted public health strategies.

papers.title_zh: 中国31个省市肾综合征出血热(HFRS)的时空分布特征及多因素发病率预测

analysis_zh.background: 本研究旨在整合多源时空数据,构建基于XGBoost和SHAP的肾综合征出血热发病率预测模型,以探讨中国肾综合征出血热发病率相关因素。
analysis_zh.methods: 将31个省份(2005‐2020)的肾综合征出血热病例数据与气候、土地利用和人口数据相结合;使用MaxEnt对啮齿动物分布进行建模;构建包含气候、土地利用、宿主和社会经济特征的XGBoost模型,并在加权省份上进行训练、验证和测试。
analysis_zh.results: 报告的肾综合征出血热病例从2005年到2020年呈下降趋势,但仍出现季节性高峰;病例主要为20‐60岁的成人;啮齿动物分布主要受最冷月最低温度和海拔影响;在剔除时间特征后,土地利用类型(森林、耕地、灌木)相对重要性超过气候变量;森林、灌木和耕地可能通过影响宿主分布和食物供给而影响传播;气候因素起间接作用;时间特征对预测仍至关重要,而土地利用和啮齿动物栖息地是关键的外源驱动因素。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究结果支持有针对性的公共卫生策略,表明土地利用和啮齿动物栖息地是肾综合征出血热风险的关键驱动因素,为监测和干预规划提供依据。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告;摘要仅提供有限的方法学细节,且未明确样本量或除省级以外的具体地点信息。
